faq.a: CVI is a chronic condition that cannot typically be cured, but its symptoms can be effectively managed with consistent conservative measures and, in some cases, surgical interventions.

Not all varicose veins indicate CVI. While varicose veins are a common manifestation, CVI refers to the broader syndrome of impaired venous return and its consequences, which can occur with or without visible varicose veins.
faq.q: Are all varicose veins a sign of CVI?

faq.a: Consistent use of graduated compression stockings and regular leg elevation are the most important self-care measures for managing CVI symptoms and preventing progression.
faq.q: What is the most important thing a patient can do to manage CVI?

ai.title: Chronic Venous Insufficiency
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) is a condition where leg veins struggle to return blood to the heart, leading to blood pooling. This results in symptoms like swelling, pain, and skin changes. It's a common cause of leg ulcers, particularly in low-resource settings.

b: Affects superficial, deep, or perforator veins.
Often a consequence of previous deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or primary valvular incompetence.
Prevalence increases with age and is higher in women.
Significant cause of morbidity and reduced quality of life.
sections.p: Chronic Venous Insufficiency (CVI) is a progressive condition affecting the venous system of the lower limbs, characterized by impaired venous return. This impairment leads to sustained venous hypertension, which in turn causes a cascade of inflammatory responses, tissue remodelling, and ultimately, the clinical manifestations observed. Understanding the underlying pathophysiology is crucial for effective diagnosis and management, especially in settings where advanced diagnostics may be limited.

b: Venous reflux: Most common cause, due to damaged or incompetent venous valves.
Venous obstruction: Less common, often from previous DVT or external compression.
Muscle pump dysfunction: Impaired calf muscle pump further exacerbates venous stasis.
Microcirculatory changes: Capillary leakage, fibrin cuff formation, and leukocyte trapping contribute to skin changes and ulceration.
CEAP classification: C0 (no visible signs) to C6 (active venous ulcer).
sections.p: The core problem in CVI is sustained venous hypertension. This occurs due to either reflux (backward flow of blood through incompetent valves) or obstruction (blockage of venous outflow). Both mechanisms lead to increased pressure in the venules and capillaries, causing fluid extravasation, inflammation, and tissue damage. The CEAP classification system (Clinical, Etiological, Anatomical, Pathophysiological) is widely used to categorize CVI severity and guide management.

b: History: Ask about leg pain (aching, heaviness, worse with standing, relieved by elevation), swelling, itching, skin changes, and previous DVT or leg trauma.

Examination: Inspect for edema (pitting), skin discoloration (hyperpigmentation, 'brawny' edema), varicose veins, lipodermatosclerosis (inverted champagne bottle appearance), and ulcers (typically medial malleolus, irregular borders, shallow, often painful).
Palpate for warmth, tenderness, and assess for pitting edema.
Trendelenburg test (if available): Helps differentiate superficial from deep venous incompetence by observing venous filling.
Ankle-brachial index (ABI): Essential to rule out co-existing peripheral arterial disease before compression therapy.
sections.p: CVI presents a significant clinical challenge, particularly in low-resource settings where late presentations and limited access to specialized care are common. Early recognition and appropriate management are vital to prevent progression to severe complications like chronic venous ulcers, which are debilitating and prone to infection. Clinicians must rely heavily on history and physical examination to establish a diagnosis and assess severity.

t.b: Does the patient have symptoms consistent with CVI? -> Aching, heaviness, swelling, skin changes, history of DVT suggest CVI.
Are there visible signs of CVI? -> Edema, varicose veins, skin changes, or ulcers confirm CVI and help stage severity.
Is there co-existing peripheral arterial disease? -> ABI less than 0.9 contraindicates or modifies compression therapy.
Is there venous reflux? -> Audible reflux on Valsalva or calf compression indicates valvular incompetence. (If unavailable, rely on clinical signs).

What is the extent and location of reflux or obstruction? -> Identifies incompetent valves, thrombus, or obstruction, guiding targeted treatment. (If unavailable, manage based on clinical severity and assume widespread incompetence).

b: Elevation: Elevate legs above heart level for 15-30 minutes several times a day to reduce edema.
Compression therapy: Cornerstone of treatment. Graduated compression stockings (20-30 mmHg or higher) reduce edema and improve venous return. Bandaging for active ulcers.
Exercise: Regular walking and calf muscle exercises improve the calf muscle pump function.
Skin care: Moisturize dry skin, treat fungal infections, and manage eczema to prevent breakdown.
Wound care: For ulcers, debridement of necrotic tissue, appropriate dressings (e.g., simple paraffin gauze, hydrocolloids if available), and infection control.
Pharmacotherapy: Diuretics for severe edema (short-term only), pentoxifylline for ulcer healing (modest benefit), antibiotics for infected ulcers (guided by local resistance patterns).
Avoid prolonged standing or sitting.
Weight management: Reduce obesity to decrease abdominal pressure on veins.
sections.p: Management of CVI is primarily conservative, focusing on reducing venous hypertension and promoting healing. In low-resource settings, emphasis is placed on affordable and accessible interventions. Surgical options are generally reserved for severe cases or when conservative measures fail, and may not be readily available.

Examiners will test your ability to diagnose CVI clinically, differentiate it from other causes of leg swelling, and outline a practical management plan, especially considering resource limitations. Be prepared to discuss the pathophysiology and the rationale behind conservative measures.

b: Not performing an ABI before compression therapy.
Confusing CVI edema with other causes of leg swelling (cardiac, renal, lymphatic).
Underestimating the impact of lifestyle modifications (elevation, exercise, weight).
Failing to address underlying causes or risk factors (e.g., obesity, prolonged standing).
Ignoring the psychological and social impact of chronic ulcers.
sections.p: Students often focus solely on varicose veins, overlooking the broader spectrum of CVI. Another common error is failing to rule out arterial disease before initiating compression, or not appreciating the importance of patient education and adherence to conservative measures.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe leg pain and swelling (suggests DVT)
Signs of infection around an ulcer (redness, warmth, pus, fever)
Rapidly worsening edema or pain despite conservative measures
New neurological deficits in the affected limb
